text:
The Pebble Index 01 BLE protocol is not in Core Devices' open-source mobile app. Their app is GPLv3 and contains only about 2000 lines of glue in libindex/, tangled with libpebble3, Firebase, Room and Koin. All actual transport lives in a closed binary, io.github.coredevices.haversine:haversine, published on Maven Central under Apache 2.0 with a private source repo.

That licence split is why the Android app depends on the binary and copies nothing from their source. Their app is GPLv3 and this repo has no LICENSE file, so copying their Kotlin would have forced this project to GPLv3. Depending on the Apache-2.0 artifact does not.

If someone later proposes vendoring or adapting their libindex/ or experimental/ modules, that is the trade being made, and it also drags in the whole Pebble watch stack.

The binary also forces the Android toolchain: its class metadata is Kotlin 2.2, so Kotlin 1.9 cannot read it, and its AAR metadata declares minCompileSdk 36. AGP was taken to the latest 8.x rather than 9.x on purpose, to avoid mixing an unrelated major migration into the same change.

Deferred, not rejected: replacing the pendant's custom pairing token with standard BLE bonding.

What the pendant does today is not encryption. It is a 16-byte bearer token sent in plaintext over an unencrypted link; the firmware calls BLEDevice::init() with no security configuration. Two consequences. A sniffer present at first pairing captures the token and can impersonate the phone forever. More importantly the token is irrelevant to eavesdropping, because the audio notifications are transmitted in the clear and can be reassembled without pairing at all.

Standard LE Secure Connections bonding would be less code than the token scheme (the token characteristic, the NVS token storage and the connection_authenticated flag would all be deleted) and would encrypt the whole link. The pendant has one button and no display, so pairing would be Just Works: protected against passive sniffing, not against an active man-in-the-middle during the pairing exchange itself.

Costs established when this was analysed: bond keys must survive the pendant's deep-sleep cold boot cycle, which needs verifying in NVS; encrypted reconnection costs a round trip against a 10 second BLE window with a 30 second hard deadline; sync.py gets harder because bonding from bleak on Linux needs a BlueZ agent; and it forces a one-time re-pair.

Bonding does not encrypt recordings at rest in LittleFS, which was judged not worth solving.

The owner chose not to do this alongside the Index work, so a failure could be attributed to one change rather than two.

Operational facts about the Index 01 ring, established by reading Core Devices' app and the vendor binary rather than from documentation.

Pairing is ordinary Android Bluetooth bonding, not an app-level token like the pendant. The bond belongs to the phone and is shared by every app on it, so once the ring is bonded this app can use it with no pairing flow of its own. That is why the ring picker just lists Android's bonded devices instead of scanning. No createBond call was written, on the basis that the bond already exists; if a bond is ever lost the ring will simply fail to connect and that is when to add it.

A ring bonds to one phone at a time. Moving it to another phone means forgetting it in Settings > Bluetooth on the old phone and then resetting the ring with an SOS button sequence (short short short, long long long, short short short).

Transfers are not destructive. The ring keeps recordings in a numbered collection buffer and each app tracks its own last successful collection index; erasing is a separate explicit call. So the official Pebble app and this app can both pull the same recordings independently. That works but is not worth relying on.

eraseCollections() and forceFailsafe() are deliberately never called anywhere in this codebase. The official app erases on pairing to clear factory test recordings; doing that here would destroy anything not yet synced.

Rings on firmware below 3.62.0 refuse to transfer until a user ID string is programmed into them. Newer firmware does not need it, so nothing was implemented. If a ring ever fails to transfer, check its firmware version before anything else.

Device selection is either/or rather than both loops at once, because one device is worn at a time and running both means continuous BLE scanning for two different advertisement types.

How to re-verify the vendor library's collection index ordering, which the ring sync design depends on.

The vendor commits the collection index BEFORE it hands us the audio for that collection. Verified by disassembling the AAR: in coredevices.haversine.HaversineTransferDelegate.handleDidFinish, the call to CollectionIndexStorage.setLastSuccessfulCollectionIndex sits at bytecode offset 120, near the start of the method, while the audio only reaches a collector much later via processMultiPartAudio / processSinglePartAudio, then emitCompleteTransfer, then MutableSharedFlow.emit.

That is why our CollectionIndexStorage serves the library from memory but defers the durable write until after the recording is saved, and why a fresh session is built per retry so the in-memory index is re-seeded from disk. Without both halves a failed save silently skips a recording forever.

To re-check after a vendor upgrade: download the haversine-android AAR from Maven Central, unzip classes.jar, and run javap -p -c on that class, then compare the offset of the setLastSuccessfulCollectionIndex call against the emitCompleteTransfer calls. If the vendor ever starts committing after the emit, the deferred-commit machinery becomes unnecessary.

Related unverified risk: the manager is given a CoroutineScope and we cannot confirm from the stripped binary that its internal coroutines stop when that scope is cancelled. Each ring session therefore owns a child scope that is cancelled and joined on teardown, with the join bounded at 3 seconds because the library ships native code and a blocking JNI call cannot be interrupted by coroutine cancellation. A warning is logged if that bound is ever hit; if it appears in logcat, the vendor is not cleaning up.

The Index 01 reports a sample rate of 9997 Hz. Confirmed on real hardware; every transfer logged the same value, so it looks like a fixed ring clock rather than something per-recording.

9997 is not a legal AAC sample rate. AAC permits only 7350, 8000, 11025, 12000, 16000, 22050, 24000, 32000, 44100, 48000, 64000, 88200 and 96000. Android's MediaCodec does NOT reject an illegal rate. Given 9997 it silently produced a track declaring 44100, while presentation timestamps were still derived from 9997, so files played back about 4.41x too fast and ffprobe reported 44100 with a container duration that looked correct. Nothing failed and nothing logged a warning.

This is why Core Devices' app resamples ring audio to 16000 before encoding. That step looks redundant if you assume the native rate is usable, and it is not.

The Android app now upsamples 9997 to 16000 by linear interpolation before encoding, and AudioEncoder has a require() that rejects any rate AAC cannot represent, so the platform can never silently coerce again. Upward was chosen because upsampling cannot alias and so needs no low-pass filter; downsampling to 8000 would have needed one.

Cost of the lesson: a backlog synced with the broken encoder produced unplayable files. They were recoverable only because the ring never deletes recordings, but re-fetching does not repair them automatically, since filenames are deterministic but the collection index had already advanced past them.

The Index 01 sends UNSIGNED 16-bit offset-binary audio samples, even though the vendor library hands them to you as a Kotlin ShortArray, which is signed. Nothing documents this. Read as signed, every sample above 32767 wraps to a large negative value, which is a near full-scale sign flip between adjacent samples and is audible as crackling. It is worst on loud consonants, because that is where the waveform crosses the wrap point.

Measured on one real 11620-sample recording:
  read as signed:   min -32768, max 32752, mean 14880, largest adjacent jump 65488
  read as unsigned: min 2192,   max 32912, mean 18828, largest adjacent jump 2896
700 samples, about 6 percent, wrapped.

The large DC offset the ring appears to have is a consequence of the same fact. Offset-binary audio has a big positive mean by construction. It is not a separate defect and chasing it on its own does not fix the crackle.

Core Devices' own removeDCBias does NOT account for this. It treats the samples as signed and only subtracts a mean, and it converts back with a narrowing toShort that truncates rather than clamps, so it can invert a loud peak into exactly the artifact it is supposed to remove. Do not reach for it thinking it is the complete answer.

How this was found, because the method mattered more than the answer. Three attempts failed while measuring the encoded M4A with ffmpeg astats. That output had already been through mean subtraction, a resampler and a lossy AAC encoder, so every measurement described our own processing rather than the ring. Dumping the raw ShortArray to a file before any processing, then pulling it with adb exec-out run-as and comparing a signed against an unsigned interpretation, answered it in a single measurement. If ring audio ever sounds wrong again, dump the raw samples first and do not reason from the encoded file.
